title: K8s OOMKilled: Why Limits Save Neighbors 💥
ig_caption:
Your pod crashes—but the real question is: who gets hurt? 💣

Here’s what happens under the hood:
• “No Limits”: one memory leak can pressure the whole node
• Kubernetes doesn’t magically protect you—memory contention spreads risk
• “Limits”: the leaky pod hits its ceiling and gets OOMKilled
• Result: 0% node RAM hostage situation—only the leaker dies
• In the visual: “0 innocent pods killed” + “neighbors evicted ✗”

Practical takeaway: Set memory requests/limits per workload so noisy neighbors can’t bring down the node. Pair it with right-sized limits and memory profiling to stop the leak early.

If one service leaks memory, would you rather “fail fast” (limits) or “fail loudly” (no limits)—and why?
fb_caption:
Resource limits are one of those “boring” settings that become life-saving the moment production gets weird.

What the animation is showing:
• In a “no limits” scenario, pods can attempt to use more memory than you intended. Under memory pressure, the node becomes the shared bottleneck. When the node runs out of memory, the failure mode can cascade—services may get evicted, restarted, or lose capacity even if they’re not the ones leaking.
• With memory limits configured, the leaky container hits its own cgroup ceiling and Kubernetes triggers an OOMKilled for that specific pod.
• Net effect: you isolate blast radius. The system prefers targeted failure (the leaker dies) over systemic failure (neighbors disrupted).

Architectural trade-offs:
• No limits:
  – Pros: fewer “false OOMs” if you’re still characterizing workloads
  – Cons: shared-node resource contention grows the blast radius; one leak can destabilize multiple workloads
• Limits:
  – Pros: deterministic blast radius; safer multi-tenant scheduling; improved incident containment
  – Cons: requires sizing discipline; too-tight limits increase restarts and latency spikes

Scalability & resilience implications:
• Requests/limits shape bin-packing. Overcommitting memory increases the odds of node-level pressure and eviction storms.
• Proper limits support predictable scheduling and reduce correlated failures—especially important when autoscaling (HPA/VPA/cluster autoscaler) is also in play.
• Limits also make autoscaling signals more meaningful: if a pod is consistently OOMKilled, you’ll see it as a scaling/optimization requirement rather than a hidden node saturation issue.

Production best practice:
1) Always set memory requests and limits for services that run continuously (especially stateful or latency-sensitive ones).
2) Start with conservative limits, observe in metrics/logs, then iteratively right-size. Treat repeated OOMKilled events as a performance bug, not just a configuration tweak.

Which approach do you default to in your org—no memory limits during early development, or strict limits everywhere—and what’s your rule for choosing the threshold?
threads_caption:
No limits = one memory leak can destabilize the whole node. Limits = the leaker hits cgroup ceiling → OOMKilled, neighbors stay safe. 💥

What’s your policy: strict limits by default, or only after profiling?
